p.src: Now in the eighth month of autumn, the first year of Zhangwu, the First Emperor led a great army to Kui Pass and encamped at White Emperor City. The vanguard had already reached the mouth of the river. A close attendant reported, “Zhuge Jin has come as an envoy from Wu.” The First Emperor ordered that he not be admitted. Huang Quan remonstrated, “Zhuge Jin’s younger brother serves as chancellor in Shu, so he must have serious business in coming. Why does Your Majesty refuse to see him? You should summon him and hear what he has to say. If his proposal can be accepted, accept it; if not, use him to carry your words back to Sun Quan, so that he may know your punitive expedition has just cause.” The First Emperor followed his counsel and summoned Zhuge Jin into the city. Zhuge Jin prostrated himself on the ground. The First Emperor asked, “Ziyu, what brings you so far?” Zhuge Jin replied, “My younger brother has long served Your Majesty, and so, heedless of the axe of execution, I have come especially to report on the affair of Jingzhou. Formerly, when Lord Guan held Jingzhou, the Marquis of Wu repeatedly sought a marriage alliance, but Lord Guan refused. Later, when Lord Guan took Xiangyang, Cao Cao repeatedly wrote to the Marquis of Wu, urging him to attack Jingzhou; the Marquis of Wu was originally unwilling, but because Lü Meng was at odds with Lord Guan, he raised troops on his own authority and mistakenly brought about this grave affair. The Marquis of Wu now regrets it, but too late. This was Lü Meng’s crime, not the Marquis of Wu’s fault. Now Lü Meng is dead, and the cause of the vendetta has passed. Lady Sun has long wished to return. The Marquis of Wu has now sent me as his envoy. He is willing to return the lady, bind and surrender the defecting generals, restore Jingzhou as before, form an everlasting alliance, and together destroy Cao Pi to punish his crime of usurpation.”

p.src: The First Emperor angrily said, “You men of Eastern Wu murdered my brother, and today you dare come here to persuade me with cunning words!” Zhuge Jin said, “Permit me to discuss with Your Majesty what is weighty and what is slight, what is great and what is small. Your Majesty is an imperial uncle of the Han. Now that the Han emperor has been usurped by Cao Pi, you do not think of destroying him, but instead abase the dignity of the sovereign of ten thousand chariots for kinship with one of another surname. This is forsaking the greater duty for the lesser. The Central Plains are the heartland of the realm, and both capitals are places where the Great Han founded its enterprise. Yet Your Majesty does not seize them and contends only for Jingzhou. This is abandoning the weighty for the slight. All beneath Heaven know that Your Majesty ascended the throne to revive the house of Han and restore its realm; yet now Your Majesty ignores Wei and instead means to attack Wu. With all respect, I cannot approve.” The First Emperor flew into a rage. “The foe who slew my brother cannot exist beneath the same Heaven as I! If you wish me to withdraw my army, only death will end the matter! Were it not for the chancellor’s sake, I would behead you first! For now I shall let you return. Tell Sun Quan to wash his neck and await the blade!” Seeing that the First Emperor would not listen, Zhuge Jin had no choice but to return to Jiangnan.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhang Zhao went to Sun Quan and said, “Zhuge Ziyu knows the armies of Shu are powerful. He therefore used a request to serve as envoy as a pretext, intending to betray Wu and enter Shu. Once gone, he will surely never return.” Sun Quan said, “Ziyu and I have sworn an unchanging bond in life and death. I will not betray Ziyu, nor will Ziyu betray me. Formerly, when Ziyu was at Chaisang and Kongming came to Wu, I wanted Ziyu to persuade him to remain. Ziyu said, ‘My brother already serves Xuande and is honor-bound to harbor no second allegiance; just as my brother will not remain, so I myself will not go to Shu.’ Those words could pierce through to the spirits. How could he be willing to surrender to Shu today? Ziyu and I may be called kindred spirits; no outsider’s words can divide us.” As he was speaking, a sudden report came that Zhuge Jin had returned. Sun Quan said, “What did I tell you?” Zhang Zhao withdrew, his face full of shame. Zhuge Jin met Sun Quan and told him that the First Emperor refused to make peace. Sun Quan was greatly alarmed. “If that is so, Jiangnan is in peril!” A man below the steps advanced and said, “I have a plan that can resolve this danger.” They looked and saw that it was the Palace Grandee Zhao Zi. Sun Quan said, “Dedu, what good plan have you?” Zhao Zi replied, “My lord may compose a memorial. I am willing to serve as envoy, go before the Wei emperor Cao Pi, explain the advantages and dangers, and induce him to attack Hanzhong. The armies of Shu will then find themselves endangered.” Sun Quan said, “That is an excellent plan. But on this mission, you must not diminish the dignity of Eastern Wu.” Zhao Zi said, “If I make the slightest error, I shall cast myself into the river and die. How could I have the face to meet the worthies of Jiangnan again?”

p.src: Sun Quan was delighted. He immediately wrote a memorial declaring himself a subject and appointed Zhao Zi as envoy. Traveling day and night, Zhao Zi reached the capital Xu, where he first met Grand Commandant Jia Xu and the other officials, high and low. At court the next morning, Jia Xu stepped from the ranks and reported, “Eastern Wu has sent Palace Grandee Zhao Zi to present a memorial.” Cao Pi laughed. “This is merely to make the armies of Shu withdraw.” He at once ordered Zhao Zi summoned. Zhao Zi prostrated himself before the vermilion steps. After Cao Pi had read the memorial, he asked Zhao Zi, “What kind of ruler is the Marquis of Wu?” Zhao Zi replied, “A ruler of intelligence, discernment, benevolence, wisdom, heroic power, and strategic vision.” Cao Pi laughed. “Is that not rather excessive praise?” Zhao Zi replied, “I do not praise him beyond his merits. That the Marquis of Wu accepted Lu Su when he was still an obscure commoner shows his intelligence; that he promoted Lü Meng from the ranks shows his discernment; that he captured Yu Jin but did not harm him shows his benevolence; that he took Jingzhou without bloodying a blade shows his wisdom; that he holds the Three Rivers and watches the realm like a tiger shows his heroic power; and that he humbles himself before Your Majesty shows his strategic vision. Judged by these things, is he not indeed a ruler of intelligence, discernment, benevolence, wisdom, heroic power, and strategic vision?” Cao Pi asked again, “Is the lord of Wu well learned?” Zhao Zi replied, “The lord of Wu commands ten thousand vessels upon the rivers and a million armored soldiers. He appoints the worthy, employs the able, and sets his mind upon great designs; whenever he has a little leisure, he reads broadly in the classics and commentaries, surveys the historical records, and extracts their essential meaning. He does not merely imitate pedants who hunt through chapters and pluck out phrases.” Cao Pi said, “I wish to attack Wu. Can it be done?” Zhao Zi replied, “A great state has armies for conquest; a small state has plans for defense.” Cao Pi asked, “Does Wu fear Wei?” Zhao Zi replied, “With a million armored soldiers and the Yangtze and Han as its moat, what has it to fear?” Cao Pi asked, “How many men like you are there in Eastern Wu?” Zhao Zi replied, “There are eighty or ninety men of exceptional intelligence and distinction; as for those of my sort, they could be measured by the cartload and bushel, too many to count.” Cao Pi sighed. “‘Sent abroad to the four quarters, he does not disgrace his lord’s commission’—you are worthy of those words.”

p.src: Cao Pi thereupon issued an edict commanding Xing Zhen, Minister of Ceremonies, to carry the patent investing Sun Quan as King of Wu and granting him the Nine Bestowments. Zhao Zi gave thanks for the imperial favor and left the city. Grandee Liu Ye remonstrated, “Sun Quan fears the might of Shu’s armies and has therefore come to submit. In my humble opinion, the warfare between Shu and Wu is Heaven’s means of destroying them. If we now send a chief general with tens of thousands of troops across the river to attack them, with Shu assaulting from without and Wei from within, Wu will perish in fewer than ten days. Once Wu has fallen, Shu will stand alone. Why does Your Majesty not act swiftly?” Cao Pi replied, “Since Sun Quan has already submitted to me with due ceremony, if I attack him, I shall discourage all beneath Heaven who wish to surrender; it is better to accept his submission.” Liu Ye said again, “Though Sun Quan possesses heroic ability, he holds only the offices of General of Agile Cavalry and Marquis of Nanchang, remnants of the Han. Because his rank is light, his power is weak, and he still fears the Central Plains; but if he is raised to kingship, he will stand only one rank below Your Majesty. Now Your Majesty believes his false surrender, exalts his rank and title, and thereby fosters his power. This is adding wings to a tiger.” Cao Pi replied, “That is not so. I shall aid neither Wu nor Shu. I shall wait and watch Wu and Shu fight. If one state destroys the other and only one remains, what difficulty will there be in eliminating it then? My mind is made up. Say no more.” He therefore ordered Xing Zhen, Minister of Ceremonies, to travel directly to Eastern Wu with Zhao Zi, bearing the patent and the ceremonial gifts.

p.src: Now Sun Quan assembled all his officials to discuss how to resist Shu, when word suddenly came that the Emperor of Wei had created their lord a king and that protocol required him to go out some distance to receive the envoy. Gu Yong remonstrated, “My lord should assume the titles of Supreme General and Lord of the Nine Provinces. You ought not accept a peerage from the Emperor of Wei.” Sun Quan replied, “In his day, the Duke of Pei accepted enfeoffment from Xiang Yu because circumstances demanded it. Why should I refuse it?” He then led all his officials outside the city to welcome the envoy. Xing Zhen, presuming upon his status as an imperial envoy from the superior realm, did not descend from his carriage upon entering the gate. Zhang Zhao flew into a rage and cried sternly, “Courtesy permits no disrespect, and law permits no want of discipline. Yet you dare act so haughtily! Do you imagine there is not so much as an inch of steel south of the Yangtze?” Xing Zhen hurriedly alighted, met Sun Quan, and entered the city beside him in another carriage. Suddenly, behind the carriages, a man burst into loud weeping and cried, “We have been unable to risk ourselves and lay down our lives so that our lord might annex Wei and swallow Shu. Instead, we have made him accept a title from another. Is this not a disgrace?” The others looked and saw that it was Xu Sheng. Xing Zhen heard him. He sighed and said, “With ministers and generals such as these in the Southland, they will not long remain beneath another!”

p.src: Now after Sun Quan had accepted his peerage and all the civil and military officials had finished offering their congratulations, he ordered fine jade, pearls, and other treasures prepared and sent a man to present them in gratitude for the imperial favor. A spy soon reported, “The ruler of Shu is advancing with the main forces of his realm, tens of thousands of foreign troops under the barbarian king Shamoke, and two contingents from Dongxi led by the Han generals Du Lu and Liu Ning. They are coming by both land and water with earthshaking might. The river force has already emerged from Wuxia, and the land force has reached Zigui.” Though Sun Quan had now ascended the royal throne, the ruler of Wei still refused to send aid. So he asked his civil and military officers, “The Shu army is very powerful. What are we to do?” All remained silent. Sun Quan sighed, “After Zhou Yu, there was Lu Su; after Lu Su, there was Lü Meng. Now Lü Meng is dead, and there is no one to share my cares!” Before he had finished, a young general suddenly strode out from the ranks, prostrated himself, and said, “Though I am young, I have studied the military classics closely. I beg several tens of thousands of troops, and I shall defeat the army of Shu.” Sun Quan looked and saw that it was Sun Huan. Sun Huan’s style name was Shuwu. His father, Sun He, had originally borne the surname Yu, but Sun Ce was fond of him and granted him the surname Sun; thus he too was counted among the kindred of the King of Wu. Sun He had four sons. Huan was the eldest. Skilled in archery and horsemanship, he had often accompanied the King of Wu on campaign, repeatedly won extraordinary merit, and been appointed Commandant of the Martial Guard; he was then twenty-five years old. Sun Quan asked, “What plan have you for defeating them?” Sun Huan replied, “I have two great generals, one named Li Yi and the other Xie Jing, each possessed of valor sufficient to withstand ten thousand men. Give me several tens of thousands of soldiers, and I shall go and capture Liu Bei.” Sun Quan said, “Though you are valiant, nephew, you are still young. You must have someone to assist you.” General of Tiger Might Zhu Ran stepped forward and said, “I am willing to join the young general in capturing Liu Bei.” Sun Quan consented. He mustered fifty thousand troops for land and water, appointed Sun Huan Commander of the Left and Zhu Ran Commander of the Right, and ordered them to march that very day. Scouts learned that the Shu army had reached Yidu and encamped. Sun Huan led twenty-five thousand troops to the approaches on the border of Yidu and divided them into three camps, one behind another, to resist the army of Shu.

p.src: Now the Shu general Wu Ban, bearing the seal of the vanguard commander, had found every place surrendering at the mere rumor of his approach since he left the Riverlands; without bloodying a blade, he advanced straight to Yidu. Learning that Sun Huan was encamped there, he sent an urgent memorial to the First Emperor. The First Emperor had by then reached Zigui. Hearing the report, he said angrily, “How dare this mere child oppose Us!” Guan Xing memorialized, “Since Sun Quan has made this boy his general, Your Majesty need not dispatch a senior commander. I am willing to go and capture him.” The First Emperor said, “I have indeed wished to see your mettle.” He immediately ordered Guan Xing to go. Guan Xing bowed farewell and was about to leave when Zhang Bao stepped forward and said, “Since Guan Xing is going to punish the rebels, I ask to accompany him.” The First Emperor said, “It is excellent that you two nephews should go together. But you must be cautious and must not act rashly.”

p.src: The two bowed farewell to the First Emperor, joined the vanguard, and advanced together, drawing up their battle formation. When Sun Huan heard that the Shu army was approaching in strength, all his camps turned out. The two armies formed facing lines. Sun Huan, with Li Yi and Xie Jing, reined in beneath his standard. From the Shu camp emerged two great generals, both in silver helmets and armor, riding white horses beneath white banners. In the place of honor, Zhang Bao leveled his eighteen-span steel-pointed spear; below him, Guan Xing held his great cleaver crosswise. Zhang Bao hurled abuse: “Sun Huan, you whelp! With death upon you, do you still dare resist the army of Heaven?” Sun Huan retorted, “Your father has already become a headless ghost, and now you too come seeking death. What utter folly!” Zhang Bao flew into a rage, leveled his spear, and charged straight at Sun Huan. From behind Sun Huan, Xie Jing spurred forward to meet him. The two generals fought for more than thirty bouts. Xie Jing fled in defeat, and Zhang Bao pursued his advantage. Seeing Xie Jing defeated, Li Yi hurriedly slapped his horse forward, swung his gilded battle-axe, and engaged Zhang Bao. Zhang Bao fought him for more than twenty bouts, with neither gaining the advantage. Tan Xiong, an assistant general in the Wu army, saw Zhang Bao’s valor and knew Li Yi could not prevail. He loosed a treacherous arrow that struck Zhang Bao’s horse squarely. Maddened by pain, the horse bolted back toward its own lines. Before it reached the main standard, it pitched to the ground and threw Zhang Bao off. Li Yi rushed forward, raised his great axe, and hacked at Zhang Bao’s head. Suddenly a red flash gleamed, and Li Yi’s head was already on the ground. Guan Xing, it appeared, had seen Zhang Bao’s horse turn back and was about to support him when he suddenly saw the horse fall and Li Yi rush forward. With a great shout, Guan Xing cut Li Yi down from his horse, rescued Zhang Bao, and pressed on to slaughter the enemy. Sun Huan suffered a crushing defeat. Each side sounded the gong and withdrew its troops.

u.src: The two bowed farewell to the First Emperor, joined the vanguard, and advanced together, drawing up their battle formation.
When Sun Huan heard that the Shu army was approaching in strength, all his camps turned out.

The two armies formed facing lines. Sun Huan, with Li Yi and Xie Jing, reined in beneath his standard. From the Shu camp emerged two great generals, both in silver helmets and armor, riding white horses beneath white banners.
In the place of honor, Zhang Bao leveled his eighteen-span steel-pointed spear; below him, Guan Xing held his great cleaver crosswise.
Zhang Bao hurled abuse: “Sun Huan, you whelp!
With death upon you, do you still dare resist the army of Heaven?”
Sun Huan retorted, “Your father has already become a headless ghost, and now you too come seeking death. What utter folly!”
Zhang Bao flew into a rage, leveled his spear, and charged straight at Sun Huan.
From behind Sun Huan, Xie Jing spurred forward to meet him.
The two generals fought for more than thirty bouts. Xie Jing fled in defeat, and Zhang Bao pursued his advantage.
Seeing Xie Jing defeated, Li Yi hurriedly slapped his horse forward, swung his gilded battle-axe, and engaged Zhang Bao.
Zhang Bao fought him for more than twenty bouts, with neither gaining the advantage.
Tan Xiong, an assistant general in the Wu army, saw Zhang Bao’s valor and knew Li Yi could not prevail. He loosed a treacherous arrow that struck Zhang Bao’s horse squarely.
Maddened by pain, the horse bolted back toward its own lines. Before it reached the main standard, it pitched to the ground and threw Zhang Bao off.
Li Yi rushed forward, raised his great axe, and hacked at Zhang Bao’s head.
Suddenly a red flash gleamed, and Li Yi’s head was already on the ground.
Guan Xing, it appeared, had seen Zhang Bao’s horse turn back and was about to support him when he suddenly saw the horse fall and Li Yi rush forward.
With a great shout, Guan Xing cut Li Yi down from his horse, rescued Zhang Bao, and pressed on to slaughter the enemy.
Sun Huan suffered a crushing defeat.
Each side sounded the gong and withdrew its troops.

p.src: The next day, Sun Huan again led out his army. Zhang Bao and Guan Xing both came forth. Guan Xing reined in before the battle line and challenged Sun Huan alone to single combat. Enraged, Sun Huan spurred forward with brandished blade and fought Guan Xing for more than thirty bouts. His strength failing, he fled back to his lines in defeat. The two young generals pursued him into the camp, while Wu Ban led Zhang Nan and Feng Xi in a sweeping attack. Zhang Bao charged valiantly at the fore and cut into the Wu army. Encountering Xie Jing, he killed him with a single thrust of his spear. The Wu troops scattered and fled. The Shu generals withdrew victorious, only to find Guan Xing missing. Zhang Bao cried in alarm, “If Anguo has come to harm, I will not live on alone!” With that, he snatched up his spear and mounted. He had searched less than a few li when he saw Guan Xing approaching, sword in his left hand and a captured general tucked alive beneath his right arm. Zhang Bao asked, “Who is this man?” Guan Xing answered with a laugh, “Amid the confusion I happened upon an enemy of mine, so I took him alive.” Zhang Bao looked and saw that it was Tan Xiong, who had loosed the treacherous arrow the day before. Overjoyed, Zhang Bao returned with him to camp, beheaded him, drained his blood, and sacrificed it to his dead horse. He then wrote a memorial and sent a man to report the victory to the First Emperor.

p.src: Having lost Li Yi, Xie Jing, Tan Xiong, and many other officers and men, Sun Huan was exhausted and isolated and could no longer withstand the enemy. He therefore sent a man back to Wu to seek aid. The Shu generals Zhang Nan and Feng Xi said to Wu Ban, “The Wu army is now beaten. This is the perfect time to take advantage of its weakness and raid the camp.” Wu Ban replied, “Though Sun Huan has lost many officers and men, Zhu Ran’s naval force remains encamped on the river and has suffered no losses. If we raid the camp today and his sailors come ashore to cut off our retreat, what shall we do?” Zhang Nan said, “That is easily dealt with. Order Generals Guan and Zhang each to lead five thousand men and lie in ambush in the mountain valleys. If Zhu Ran comes to the rescue, the two forces can strike from left and right and surely prevail.” Wu Ban said, “Better first send a common soldier pretending to be a deserter and have him reveal our plan to raid the camp to Zhu Ran. When he sees the fires rise, Zhu Ran will surely come to the rescue. Then our ambush can attack him, and the great affair will be accomplished.” Feng Xi and the others were delighted and carried out the plan.

p.src: Now Zhu Ran, hearing that Sun Huan had lost troops and generals, was about to go to his aid when the soldiers lying in ambush along the road brought several common soldiers aboard his ship to surrender. When Zhu Ran questioned them, one soldier said, “We served under Feng Xi. Because rewards and punishments were administered unjustly, we have come expressly to surrender and to reveal a secret.” Zhu Ran asked, “What have you come to report?” The soldier replied, “Tonight Feng Xi intends to take advantage of your unpreparedness and raid General Sun’s camp. The signal agreed upon is the lighting of a fire.” Having heard this, Zhu Ran immediately sent a man to inform Sun Huan. But halfway there, the messenger was slain by Guan Xing. Meanwhile, Zhu Ran consulted his officers, intending to lead troops to Sun Huan’s aid. His subordinate general Cui Yu said, “We cannot place complete trust in the word of common soldiers. Should anything go awry, both our land and naval forces will be utterly lost. You should remain here and securely defend the naval camp; I am willing to make the journey in your stead.” Zhu Ran accepted his proposal and ordered Cui Yu to set out with ten thousand troops. That night Feng Xi, Zhang Nan, and Wu Ban divided their forces into three columns and charged straight into Sun Huan’s camp as fires sprang up on every side. The troops of Wu fell into great confusion and fled wherever they could find a way out.

p.src: Meanwhile, as Cui Yu marched on, he suddenly saw the fires rise and urgently pressed his troops forward. He had only just rounded the mountain when drums suddenly thundered through the valley; Guan Xing attacked from the left and Zhang Bao from the right, assailing him from both sides. Cui Yu was greatly alarmed and was about to flee when he came face-to-face with Zhang Bao; after no more than a single mounted exchange, Zhang Bao captured him alive and returned. When Zhu Ran learned how desperate the situation was, he sent his ships downstream and retreated some fifty or sixty li. Sun Huan led his defeated troops in flight and asked his officers, “What city ahead has strong walls and ample provisions?” One officer replied, “Directly north of here lies the city of Yiling, where we can station our forces.” Sun Huan hastily led his defeated army toward Yiling. He had only just entered the city when Wu Ban and the others arrived in pursuit and completely surrounded it. Guan Xing, Zhang Bao, and the others escorted Cui Yu back to Zigui. The First Ruler was overjoyed. He had Cui Yu beheaded and richly rewarded the entire army. From then on, his awesome might shook the land, and every general south of the Yangtze trembled with fear.

p.src: Now Sun Huan sent a man to appeal to the King of Wu for aid. Greatly alarmed, the king immediately summoned his civil and military officers and said, “Sun Huan is now besieged at Yiling, while Zhu Ran has suffered a crushing defeat on the river. The forces of Shu are overwhelming—what are we to do?” Zhang Zhao submitted, “Though many of our generals have passed away, more than ten still remain. Why should we fear Liu Bei? Appoint Han Dang commander-in-chief, Zhou Tai his deputy, Pan Zhang as vanguard, Ling Tong to guard the rear, and Gan Ning as support, and send an army of one hundred thousand to resist him.” Sun Quan accepted the proposal and immediately ordered the generals to depart with all speed. At this time Gan Ning was suffering from dysentery, yet he joined the expedition despite his illness.

p.src: Meanwhile, from Wu Gorge and Jianping all the way to the borders of Yiling, the First Ruler established more than forty linked camps extending over seventy-odd li; seeing Guan Xing and Zhang Bao repeatedly distinguish themselves, he sighed, “All the generals who once followed me have grown old and are no longer of use; but with two nephews so heroic as these, why should I have any fear of Sun Quan!” While he was still speaking, a sudden report came that Han Dang and Zhou Tai had arrived at the head of their troops. Just as the First Ruler was about to send a general to meet the enemy, a close attendant reported, “The veteran general Huang Zhong has taken five or six men and gone over toward Eastern Wu.” The First Ruler laughed and said, “Huang Hansheng is no traitor; because I let slip the mistaken remark that old men are useless, he must have refused to yield to age and gone to strive against the enemy.” He immediately summoned Guan Xing and Zhang Bao and said, “Huang Hansheng is certain to meet with danger on this venture. My worthy nephews, do not shrink from the hardship, but go and assist him. As soon as he has won even some small merit, you may order him to return, and must not allow any harm to befall him.” The two young generals took leave of the First Ruler and led their own troops forth to assist Huang Zhong.
